newsitem.title: USA: Oil prices soar on refinery problems, storm.
newsitem.headline: Oil prices soar on refinery problems, storm.

text.p: Oil prices soared on Monday, led by worries about a tropical storm threatening to disrupt tanker deliveries in the Gulf of Mexico and on news of curtailed output due to maintenance at refineries.
On top of those supply problems, colder weather in the Northeast over the weekend added to concerns about low heating oil stocks.
"Basically, the sky's the limit," said Tom Bentz, energy analyst at ING Derivatives in New York. "It's low stocks, cold weather, and it's technical strength."

Tropical Storm Josephine, with 70 mph winds, was centred 175 miles south southwest of Apalachicola, Fla., late Monday and was likely to reach hurricane strength by the evening, weather forecasters said.

The Louisiana Offshore Oil Port, or LOOP, has been shut since Saturday due to the storm but was expected to reopen later this week. Nevertheless, the weather was expected to halt some oil production in the Gulf of Mexico, traders said.
The delay of four to five crude tankers waiting to deliver at the LOOP, the largest offshore U.S. unloading point, fed buying at the New York Mercantile Exchange.
November crude oil at NYMEX closed 51 cents higher at $25.24 a barrel after rising to a contract high of $25.28.

Oil traders also said there were problems with a catalytic cracker, which makes lighter products such as gasoline, at BP America Inc.'s 231,500 barrel-a-day refinery in Belle Chasse, La. There was no comment from the company.
"There has been a whole series of maintenance turnarounds," said analyst Tim Evans at Pegasus Econometric Group.

November unleaded gasoline closed up 2.71 cents to 66.34 cents a gallon, hitting a contract high of 66.50 cents late in the day. November heating oil ended 2.06 cents higher at 76.49 cents a gallon after reaching a contract high of 76.65 cents.
Among other refiners, Sun Oil Co. said it would proceed with planned maintenance at its 175,000 barrel-a-day refinery at Marcus Hook, Pa., from Oct. 4.
Sun will also idle a crude distillation unit for 18 days and a catalytic cracker for 44 days.
Heating oil prices have risen more than 30 percent in the last three months on historically low inventories as the United States, the world's largest heating oil consumer, heads into the winter.

In other markets, grain prices rose at the Chicago Board of Trade as cold rainy weather in the eastern Corn Belt continued to delay harvesting. Crop forecaster Conrad Leslie estimated a smaller-than-expected corn crop.
November soybeans closed 7 cents a bushel higher at $7.34-1/4, and December corn ended 3-1/4 cents a bushel higher at $2.92-3/4.

The Leslie survey, based on monthly estimates from 1,200 Midwest grain elevators, pegged 1996 U.S. corn production at 8.906 billion bushels, below the roughly 9 billion bushel level predicted recently by several other market watchers.
"The 8.906 was a little below what the trade had expected and maybe was a little supportive," said Mark Cermak, analyst for O'Connor and Co.

Soybeans were supported in part by a report from Hong Kong traders that China had purchased between 120,000 to 150,000 metric tons of soybean meal last week, to be divided among South American suppliers, the United States and India.
"We're also starting to hear talk soybean yields in Iowa are a little lower than expected," said another O'Connor analyst, Ron Kucha.
